title: A rare case of dengue encephalopathy complicating a term pregnancy
case_prompt:
A 28-year-old woman at 37 weeks’ gestation presented with a 4-day history of fever. On day 5 she became irritable, somnolent, and aggressive, and subsequently unresponsive to commands. Examination revealed T 38.5 °C, anicteric sclerae, no pallor, and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 9 (E2 V2 M5). Respiratory, cardiovascular, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. There was no neck stiffness; Kernig’s and Brudzinski’s signs were negative. Cranial nerves were intact, and there were no pyramidal or extrapyramidal signs. Fundoscopy showed no papilledema.

Laboratory studies on admission:
- White cell count 9,000 cells/mm3; hemoglobin 10 g/dL; mean corpuscular volume 85 fL; platelet count 60,000 cells/mm3, falling to 8,000 cells/mm3; hematocrit 33%.  
- ESR 20 mm/h; C-reactive protein 4 mg/dL; LDH < 200 U/L.  
- Peripheral blood film: thrombocytopenia without microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.  
- Urinalysis: no proteinuria or hematuria.  
- Aspartate aminotransferase 25 U/L rising to 250 U/L; alanine aminotransferase 20 U/L rising to 250 U/L; alkaline phosphatase 300 U/L; total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL.  
- Renal function and serum electrolytes were normal.  
- Coagulation profile: PT 10 s, APTT 38 s, INR 1.2, fibrin-degradation products < 0.2 U/L.  
- Ultrasound scan: no pleural effusions or ascites.  
- Dengue NS1 antigen was positive on illness day 4; dengue IgM antibodies were high in titer by day 6.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Dengue hemorrhagic fever with vascular leakage causing cerebral edema — “Ultrasound scan did not reveal any pleural effusions or ascites excluding the early signs of capillary vascular leakage.”  
2. Dengue shock–related cerebral hypoperfusion — “Respiratory, cardiovascular and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.”  
3. Disseminated intravascular coagulation — “Clotting profile was PT 10 s, APTT 38 s, INR 1.2 and FDP < 0.2 u/L, excluding the possibility of disseminated intravascular coagulation.”  
4. Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (TTP/HELLP) — “Blood picture revealed a thrombocytopenia in keeping with a possible viral infection, there were no features of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.”  
5. Preeclampsia/HELLP syndrome — “Urine analysis excluded proteinuria and hematuria.”  
6. Intracranial hemorrhage — “Cranial nerves were intact. Pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs were absent.”  
7. Electrolyte derangements causing encephalopathy — “Renal functions and serum electrolytes were normal.”  
8. Hepatic encephalopathy — “serum bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL” with normal synthetic function argued against fulminant hepatic failure.  
9. Other viral encephalitides (e.g., Japanese encephalitis) — “Japanese encephalitis virus ... characteristically produces bilateral thalamic involvement ... and can be confirmed by a CSF study.”  
10. Dengue encephalopathy — “serology was strongly positive for dengue infection and with the present dengue epidemic in our country we strongly suspected dengue encephalopathy as our first differential diagnosis.”
